samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are strong and give closely matching advice. B ranks the work more clearly by giving each item an effort size and tying cuts to how often patients repeat them (the tab slide as the most frequent interaction). It also handles the password shake more fully, with its own reduced-motion fallback, keeping the text error on screen and returning focus to the password field. A is tight and well reasoned, but it covers reduced motion only in general terms and assumes, without data, that the patient base skews older. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are strong, ranked and cover the rubric well. A is a little ahead because it ties the tab-slide cut directly to repeated use, gives the shake its own reduced-motion fallback, and adds useful detail on effort and handling interrupted clicks. B ranks the lab-result cue sensibly high, but it guesses that the patient base skews older, and its reason for the tab change rests more on spatial meaning than on how often the tabs get used.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a clear ranked order and cover the same core fixes: adding save and lab-result feedback, cutting the slide, stagger and bounce, and keeping the refill checkmark. B ties its cuts more explicitly to repeated use (the tab switch as the most frequent action, the bounce replaying every visit) and adds a 'Not adding' list. It also gives reduced-motion handling item by item. A is tighter, which suits the 'don't pad it' request, but it is a little thinner on these points. Each answer makes one small unsupported inference: A says the users skew older, and B calls the tab switch the most frequent action. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a sound ranked audit that covers the same main points. A explains its cuts more clearly in terms of repeated use: the tab switch is the most frequent action, and the logo replays on every visit. A also gives specific reduced-motion handling for each kept animation and has an explicit 'Not adding' list. B is tighter, but it asserts without support that 'your users skew older', which is unsupported usage data, and its reason for cutting the tab slide is less tied to repeated use.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover the same ground well: cut the slide, the stagger and the bounce, add feedback for the save and the lab results, tone down the shake, and keep the refill checkmark with checks. B edges ahead because it has explicit 'Leave alone' and 'Not adding' sections, separates quick deletions from the real release work, and gives more careful reduced-motion guidance. Against B: it is wordier, which works against 'don't pad it'. It also calls items 3 and 4 the 'biggest gap' and 'most important change' while ranking them below the cuts, which muddles its ranking. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover the same ground well: they cut the slide, the stagger and the bounce, add feedback for the save and the lab results, keep the refill checkmark, soften the shake and add reduced-motion handling. B's ranking is internally consistent and tighter, which fits 'don't pad it'. A calls lab results 'the most important change' yet ranks them fourth, though it adds a useful 'not adding' list and an explicit afternoon-versus-release order of attack.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say plainly that most of the board shouldn't animate, give a ranked list of change-signalling cues, and suggest good wording for the owner. A is more concrete: it gives durations and easing for nearly every cue, puts a number on the cost of motion across 200 assignments a shift, and explains each item it rules out in terms of the dispatcher's speed and fatigue. B is slightly tighter but leaves out durations for several of its cues. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers reject decorative motion, name specific cues with durations, and give a good line for the owner. A does it more concisely, and its rule 'never move rows out from under the cursor' is cleaner than B's animated row insert and removal. B's 200-repetitions cost math is a strong point, but its effort ratings, extra items and longer pushback list make it read more like a catalog.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers turn down decorative motion and give a short list of state-change cues with durations. A is more careful about a dispatcher's speed: it warns that collapsing or re-sorting rows can move targets under the cursor, and it rules out animated reordering. B recommends animated reflow and a slide from the job side to the driver side, which carry that same risk. B is more proportionate and adds useful ideas (capping simultaneous flashes and testing a prototype with dispatchers), but A's direct, no-delay framing for the owner and its clearer list of what to keep static give it a slight edge, even though it reads more like a catalog. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers turn down decorative motion and offer specific, justified cues with durations. A is shorter and more in proportion, and its owner framing ('current and trustworthy', plus a test with real dispatchers) is practical. B is thorough but grows into a five-item ranked catalog with handoff specs, so it is less proportionate, although its framing for the owner is strong and it says more about what to keep static.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers reject decorative motion and recommend a small set of functional cues with durations, but A is tighter. A's owner framing is also more concrete: it contrasts 'delightful' with 'trustworthy and current' and adds a live/last-updated indicator. B is thorough, with good interruptibility and performance constraints, but its effort ratings, table and handoff section push it toward a catalog, and the slide-in drawer is a weaker inclusion. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A says outright to animate four things and leave everything else static. It gives every cue a duration and spec, and its skip table explains each exclusion in terms of dispatcher speed, mis-clicks and fatigue late in a shift. B is also sound and frames the pitch to the owner better ('trustworthy and current', plus a live indicator), but some of its cues have no durations and its 'say no' list mostly gives no reasons. Both answers are a bit long for the question.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers correctly find the real visibility bug that hides the close animation and the reduced-motion specificity gap. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B gives precise, short timings for the highlight and its fade, uses tabular numerals to prevent layout shift, and batches several changes from one refresh into a single cue and a single announcement. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover the main points: update values in place, use tabular numerals, never reorder or auto-scroll, leave a temporary marker for people who looked away, avoid replaying animations after a tab wakes, and respect reduced motion. A's wicket line stays until the next event, which comes closer to a persistent cue, and its batching advice is brief. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover the main points well: change only the cells that changed, never reorder or auto-scroll, use tabular numerals, add a non-motion marker and respect reduced motion. A wins because it gives more exact timings in a spec table, says plainly not to stagger or escalate when several values change at once, and includes a CSS sketch. B's timings are looser (2–3 s, 60–90 s), and its wicket line stays until the next event.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give similar sound advice: highlight only the changed cell, keep the layout still, use an off-screen pill, add aria-live for wickets only, and make sound opt-in. A is more concrete, with exact durations, CSS, a spec table covering interrupts and reduced motion, and a pause control. B does well on hidden tabs and starred matches, but its timings are looser ranges and it has no implementation detail. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend highlighting only the changed values, keeping the layout fixed, using a pill for off-screen changes, polite aria-live announcements for wickets only, and opt-in sound. B is better on timing: it gives exact durations, says never to pulse, and includes a full spec table with interrupt and reduced-motion behaviour. It also adds a pause control and suggests not highlighting secondary stats at all. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make the same sound per-candidate decisions, keep cues for events that happen while the customer isn't looking, and cover toggles, OS silent/DND settings and visible fallbacks. A is tighter and makes a couple of sharper calls: it sends 'heading out' only after 'I'm here', and it marks only that alert as time-sensitive. A also comes closer to the testing point by asking to check that the ready chime fires reliably. Neither answer clearly says that vibration and sound support varies by device and browser, or that it needs testing on real devices, and B is longer than a team thread needs despite good extras like avoiding double alerts. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both give clear per-candidate decisions, favor alerts that reach someone who isn't looking, and cover toggles, silent mode/DND and pairing every cue with something visible. B edges ahead with practical details: it fires the haptic only after the server confirms, sends 'heading out' only after 'I'm here', and tells the team to check that the chime fires reliably. That last point comes closest to admitting device support varies, though neither answer says outright to test on real devices. B overstates when it calls sound 'the only way to reach them', and A's data plan for settling the disagreement is a nice touch, but B is slightly more actionable overall.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make clear decisions per candidate and keep sound and vibration for the ready and heading-out moments. A explicitly covers Do Not Disturb and reduced-haptics settings, adds a useful note on not encouraging phone use while driving, and is a bit shorter. B gives more platform detail (time-sensitive interruption level, Android channels) but leaves out DND and runs longer. Neither says plainly that device and browser support for sound and vibration varies; both only advise real-device testing in a car. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): The two answers are very close: both give a verdict for each candidate, keep sound and vibration for 'order ready' and 'staff heading out', and say to test in a real car. B edges ahead because it names Do Not Disturb and reduced-haptics settings explicitly and adds a useful point about not prompting phone use while driving. A is a little more decisive on the jingle, and B's 'do three' opening is slightly muddled. Neither answer says outright that vibration and sound support differs across devices and browsers.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a clear verdict per candidate and keep sound and vibration for the order-ready and staff-heading-out moments. A argues more firmly against the order-placed jingle and states the accessibility rule more plainly: a cue is never the only signal, with deaf and hard-of-hearing users and muted phones named. B adds useful API detail but turns the jingle into a haptic, which gives away part of the case against it. Neither says that device support varies or that cues should be tested on real devices. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both give a clear verdict for each candidate, keep sound and vibration for the two moments when the customer isn't looking, and reject the buzz on every button. B rejects the jingle outright and covers more of the safeguards: an in-app off switch, silent mode and Do Not Disturb, and never relying on the cue alone, with accessibility as a reason. Neither answer says that support varies by device or that cues need testing on real phones, so both score low on item 4.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers define tight token sets, map every requested pattern, and say clearly what may and may not animate. B's reduced-motion column per pattern is better, though A's version contradicts itself: it zeroes `fast` but then allows `fast` fades. A wins on being usable documentation: it explicitly calls the numbers a starting proposal to tune and says how to request new tokens, while B adds unrequested material (optimistic updates, error handling, toast timing) and never frames its values as tunable. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers have clean token sets and clear mappings from pattern to value. A's preset table, with a reduced-motion column for each pattern, is the stronger lookup. B does better on what should not animate: background data refresh, expand-all, tabs and filters, navigation chrome and focus rings. B also says the numbers are starting points to try and tune, while A adds scope such as waiting states, errors and toast timing, and never frames its values as adjustable. B's reduced-motion section is slightly inconsistent: it sets the `fast` duration to 0ms but then says a short `fast` fade is fine.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B is the better answer overall: it has a cleaner token set (four durations, three easings), says outright that the numbers are starting points to tune, and has a short, clear process for changing them, which makes it easy to use as documentation. A is more thorough, with a reduced-motion fallback for each pattern and an explicit list of what not to animate. But it uses literal values like 160ms, 120ms and 1000ms even though its own checklist bans literal values, it is too long for quick lookup, and it never says the numbers are meant to be tuned. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): A gives a tight, consistent token set (4 durations, 3 easings) and a clear recipe per pattern, so a developer can actually use it as documentation, along with a short process for proposing changes. B is more thorough and has an excellent per-preset reduced-motion column and a don't-animate list. However, it breaks its own 'no literal ms' rule (120ms, 160ms, 150ms, 1000ms in the table) and grows well past the request with loading, error, and live-data guidance. A's reduced-motion rule is global rather than spelled out per pattern, which is its main weakness.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers define a tight set of four duration tokens and three easings and map all six patterns in a lookup table. B wins mainly on reduced motion: its component table says what each pattern does instead, and its overrides are complete. A leaves the side-panel reduced-motion keyframe as an unfinished placeholder. B also has a clearer 'what we don't animate' list, but it is noticeably longer, with error handling, optimistic updates and other content beyond motion, plus some meta chatter about the Write tool, so A is tighter as documentation. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a small set of tokens and a clear component table. A is better on reduced motion: it has a per-pattern reduced-motion column and working override CSS. B's reduced-motion block points to a keyframe it never defines, and setting `grid-template-rows: 1fr` would leave collapsed rows taking up space. A strays into errors, optimistic updates and live updates, which makes it longer, but its core motion guidance is more complete and reliable.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep the old results and pins visible, place indicators in the filter bar, list and map, use 300ms and 1s thresholds, and handle failure with stale results, a plain-language banner and Retry. B only says to swap the count and cards together, though it adds useful extras such as a silent auto-retry and a first-load failure state. A adds a good first-load failure state, but it is slightly thinner on reserving space.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep fast loads silent, use a 300ms threshold and handle failure well with the old results kept, a plain-language banner and Retry. A wins narrowly because it never removes the stale results and limits skeletons to the first load. B swaps the dimmed cards for skeletons after 1.5s, which hides useful content and adds a second swap that can cause layout shift. B does mark loading more clearly on the map with its floating pill and adds useful extras like automatic retry and a 10s timeout. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep stale content visible, use timing thresholds and specify a strong failure state with a plain-language banner and Retry. B is more consistent. It never swaps stale results for skeletons, keeps skeletons for the first load only, reserves space for the error banner and animates only opacity and transform. A replaces the dimmed cards with skeletons after 1.5s, which partly blanks the previous results. A does have a more explicit map-side indicator and failure notice.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A keeps the old list and pins visible for the whole load. It also says clearly when skeletons belong: only on first load or after a jump to a new area, when there's nothing old to show. B swaps the cards for skeletons after 1s, which throws away the previous results and partly defeats its own keep-the-old-results principle. B does have a slightly better map indicator (the 'Updating homes…' pill), and both handle failure well. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Answer B keeps the old results on screen for the whole wait and limits skeletons to first loads or a jump to a new area, which handles both stale-content and layout-shift concerns well. Answer A swaps the cards for skeletons after 1s, which removes the old results during exactly the slow loads where they matter most and contradicts its own principle. Both answers treat failure well, and A's map pill gives a slightly clearer loading signal on the map.
